questions.title: Western Cape Holiday — Map Reading, Scale, Luggage Policy and Time

subQuestions.questionText: A map of the Western Cape shows its travel regions as different coloured areas, plus cities, towns and roads. Into how many regions is the Western Cape divided?
subQuestions.memoText:
6

[Award 2 marks for reading the map correctly]

subQuestions.questionText: Identify two oceans shown on the map.
subQuestions.memoText:
South Atlantic Ocean (Atlantic Ocean) and Indian Ocean

[Award 2 marks — 1 per ocean]

subQuestions.questionText: Name two provinces that border the Western Cape.
subQuestions.memoText:
Northern Cape and Eastern Cape

[Award 2 marks — 1 per province]

subQuestions.questionText: Give the type of scale used on this map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Bar scale (also accept: line scale / linear scale)

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: Steve Peters travels from Cape Town to Knysna. Use a ruler to measure, to the nearest millimetre, the straight-line distance from Cape Town to Knysna on the map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Approximately 111 mm (accept 110 mm – 113 mm), i.e. 11,1 cm (11,0 cm – 11,3 cm), measured on the printed version.

Mark 1: using a ruler to measure the straight-line distance
Mark 2: a value in the accepted range

subQuestions.label: 1.2.2 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: Identify the road that Steve Peters should travel to get from Cape Town to Knysna.
subQuestions.memoText:
The N2

[Award 2 marks for the correct road name]

subQuestions.label: 1.2.2 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: What does the letter N stand for on the road marked N9?
subQuestions.memoText:
National (route/road)

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: Name TWO tourist attractions that Steve Peters will be able to visit in Knysna.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any two of: Knysna Elephant Park; Garden Route National Park (Knysna Lake Area / Tsitsikamma NP / Wilderness NP).

[Award 2 marks — 1 per correct attraction]

subQuestions.questionText: FlySafair's fare covers two free carry-on bags (the larger not more than 7 kg). A 20 kg checked-in bag can be added for R155. Calculate the luggage fees if Steve Peters brings: a laptop bag weighing 3 kg, a 7 kg suitcase and a 19,5 kg suitcase. He aims to fully use the airline's luggage allowance.
subQuestions.memoText:
The 3 kg laptop bag and the 7 kg suitcase are carried as the two free carry-on bags.
The 19,5 kg suitcase must be checked in (it is under 20 kg) at a cost of R155.
Luggage fees = R155

Mark 1: recognising the 19,5 kg bag must be checked in
Mark 2: answer R155

subQuestions.questionText: Convert the maximum weight of checked-in luggage (20 kg) to grams.
subQuestions.memoText:
20 kg × 1 000 = 20 000 grams

Mark 1: multiplying by 1 000
Mark 2: answer 20 000 grams

subQuestions.label: 1.3.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: Steve Peters calculated the volume of his checked-in luggage. Explain the meaning of volume.
subQuestions.memoText:
Volume is the amount of space that a 3-dimensional (3D) object takes up or can hold.

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.label: 1.3.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Which is the correct formula for the volume of a rectangular prism?
subQuestions.memoText:
C — Volume = length × width × height

[Award 2 marks for identifying option C]

subQuestions.label: 1.3.3 (c)
subQuestions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a correct unit of measurement for volume or capacity?
subQuestions.memoText:
D — cm²

(cm² is a unit of area. Volume and capacity use cubic units or litre-based units: cm³, mℓ, m³.)

[Award 2 marks for identifying option D]

subQuestions.label: 1.4.1 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: Steve Peters' boarding pass is shown for his flight from Johannesburg to Cape Town. Determine the estimated departure time of Steve's flight from Johannesburg (JHB).
subQuestions.memoText:
13:00 (1:00 pm)

[Award 2 marks for reading the boarding pass correctly]

subQuestions.label: 1.4.1 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Write down, in words, the time Steve's flight landed in Cape Town (CPT).
subQuestions.memoText:
Ten past three (in the afternoon) — i.e. fifteen ten / 15:10.

[Award 2 marks for writing the landing time correctly in words]

subQuestions.questionText: Steve's flight was delayed and only landed at 15:45. Describe how you would display this time on an analogue clock face (with the hour hand shorter than the minute hand).
subQuestions.memoText:
Minute hand pointing to the 9 (45 minutes).
Hour hand between the 3 and the 4, closer to the 4.
(Lose a mark if both hands are in the correct place but drawn the same length.)

Mark 1: minute hand on 9
Mark 2: hour hand between 3 and 4

questions.title: Dumisani's Garden Chess Board — Area, Decking Boards, Tiles and Paint

subQuestions.questionText: Dumisani is building a garden chess board with a picture and an aerial view of the finished garden shown. Explain the meaning of aerial view.
subQuestions.memoText:
An aerial view is what you see when you look at something from directly above (a bird's-eye view / top view).

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: The chess board (without the wooden deck border) is a square of side 2,8 m. Calculate, in m², the area of the chess board without the wooden deck border. Use: Area of rectangle = length × breadth.
subQuestions.memoText:
Area = 2,8 m × 2,8 m = 7,84 m²

Mark 1: substituting 2,8 × 2,8
Mark 2: answer 7,84 m²

subQuestions.label: 2.1.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: The outer edge of the wooden deck measures 157,48 inches. Show, rounded to the nearest cm, that the length of the wooden deck is 400 cm, if 1 inch = 2,54 cm.

subQuestions.label: 2.1.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Calculate, in m², the area taken up by the wooden deck surrounding the chessboard. The outer square is 400 cm × 400 cm and the chessboard is 2,8 m × 2,8 m. Use: Area of rectangle = length × breadth.
subQuestions.memoText:
Outer square = 400 cm × 400 cm = 4 m × 4 m = 16 m²
Deck area = outer area − chessboard area = 16 m² − 7,84 m² = 8,16 m²

Mark 1: converting 400 cm to 4 m
Mark 2: 4 × 4 = 16 m²
Mark 3: subtracting the chessboard area
Mark 4: answer 8,16 m²

subQuestions.label: 2.1.4 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: The outer square of the deck is 4 m and the chess board is 2,8 m. Using calculations, show that the width of the wooden deck strip around the chess board is 600 mm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Total deck width across the square = 4 m − 2,8 m = 1,2 m
This is shared by the two strips (one on each side), so each strip = 1,2 m ÷ 2 = 0,6 m
0,6 m × 1 000 = 600 mm ✓

Mark 1: 4 m − 2,8 m = 1,2 m
Mark 2: ÷ 2 → 0,6 m
Mark 3: converting to 600 mm

subQuestions.label: 2.1.4 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Each single decking board is 1 700 mm long and 120 mm wide. The deck strip around each side is 600 mm wide, and the usable length of each side strip is 4 000 mm − 600 mm = 3 400 mm (so pieces do not overlap at the corners). Calculate the number of single decking boards Dumisani will need to complete his deck (assembled as in Figure 1).
subQuestions.memoText:
Along the length of one side strip: 3 400 mm ÷ 1 700 mm = 2 boards
Across the width of one side strip: 600 mm ÷ 120 mm = 5 boards
Boards per side = 2 × 5 = 10
Total for all 4 sides = 10 × 4 = 40 boards

Mark 1: 4 000 − 600 = 3 400 mm
Mark 2: 3 400 ÷ 1 700 = 2
Mark 3: 600 ÷ 120 = 5
Mark 4: 2 × 5 per side
Mark 5: × 4 sides
Mark 6: answer 40 boards

subQuestions.label: 2.1.4 (c)
subQuestions.questionText: Each decking board costs R260 excluding VAT. Using your answer from Question 2.1.4 (b) (40 boards), calculate the total cost of the decking, including 15% VAT.
subQuestions.memoText:
Cost excluding VAT = 40 × R260 = R10 400
Cost including VAT = R10 400 × 1,15 = R11 960

Mark 1: 40 × R260
Mark 2: × 1,15 (VAT-inclusive)
Mark 3: answer R11 960

subQuestions.questionText: The chessboard has 64 squares. Each player in a game of chess has 16 pieces. Calculate the total number of unoccupied squares on the chessboard when all the pieces are placed, each on a separate square, on both sides of the board.
subQuestions.memoText:
Unoccupied squares = 64 − 16 − 16 = 32

Mark 1: 64 total squares
Mark 2: subtracting 16 + 16 pieces
Mark 3: answer 32

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the number of white and the number of black ceramic floor tiles Dumisani needs to purchase to complete the 64-square chessboard.
subQuestions.memoText:
A chessboard has equal numbers of light and dark squares: 64 ÷ 2 = 32.
White = 32
Black = 32

Mark 1: White = 32
Mark 2: Black = 32

subQuestions.questionText: Dumisani cannot find enough black tiles, so he will paint the 32 required black tiles with two coats of paint. Each tile is 350 mm by 350 mm. The Plascon Stoep Enamel comes in a 1-litre can with a spread rate of 14,3 m²/litre. Show, using calculations, whether Dumisani's statement that he will only need one can of paint for two coats is correct. Use: Area of square = side × side.
subQuestions.memoText:
Area of one tile = 0,35 m × 0,35 m = 0,1225 m²
Area of 32 tiles = 0,1225 × 32 = 3,92 m²
Two coats = 3,92 × 2 = 7,84 m²
One can covers 14,3 m², and 7,84 m² < 14,3 m²
Therefore one can is enough — Dumisani's statement is correct.

Mark 1: 350 mm = 0,35 m
Mark 2: 0,35 × 0,35 = 0,1225 m²
Mark 3: × 32
Mark 4: 3,92 m²
Mark 5: × 2 (two coats)
Mark 6: 7,84 m²
Mark 7: comparing to 14,3 m² and concluding one can is enough

questions.title: Centre Pivot Irrigation — Circle Area, Pythagoras, Circumference and Volume

subQuestions.questionText: The Agrico G4 centre pivot system is built from 70 m sections connected together. Piet Cronjé has connected five of these 70 m sections together to form one long irrigation arm. Calculate the total length of the irrigation arm he has created.
subQuestions.memoText:
Total length = 70 m × 5 = 350 m

Mark 1: 70 × 5
Mark 2: answer 350 m

subQuestions.questionText: Using your answer from Question 3.1.1 (350 m as the radius), calculate, in m², the total area of the circular field that Piet Cronjé has under irrigation. Use: Area of a circle = π × radius², with π = 3,142.
subQuestions.memoText:
Area = 3,142 × 350²
= 3,142 × 122 500
= 384 895 m²

Mark 1: radius = 350 m
Mark 2: substituting into the formula
Mark 3: answer 384 895 m²

subQuestions.questionText: Using your answer from Question 3.1.2, convert, to one decimal place, the area of the circular field (384 895 m²) to hectares. Note: 1 hectare = 10 000 m².
subQuestions.memoText:
= 384 895 ÷ 10 000
= 38,4895
= 38,5 hectares

Mark 1: dividing by 10 000
Mark 2: 38,4895
Mark 3: rounding to 1 decimal place → 38,5 ha

subQuestions.questionText: An irrigation tower is supported above the ground. In the diagram (all lengths in feet), a support brace forms a right-angled triangle with a hypotenuse of 12 feet and a vertical side of 9 feet; the length A to B spans two of the horizontal sides. Calculate, in metres, the length from A to B, rounded to the nearest metre, if 1 foot = 0,3048 metres. Use: a² + b² = c² (Pythagoras' Theorem).
subQuestions.memoText:
Horizontal side: a² = 12² − 9² = 144 − 81 = 63
a = √63 = 7,94 feet
A to B = 2 × 7,94 = 15,87 feet
In metres = 15,87 × 0,3048 = 4,84 m ≈ 5 m

Mark 1: 12² − 9²
Mark 2: = 63
Mark 3: a = 7,94 feet
Mark 4: doubling → 15,87 feet
Mark 5: × 0,3048
Mark 6: answer ≈ 5 m

subQuestions.questionText: Each tyre on the wheels of the irrigation tower has a diameter of 1 160 mm. Calculate, in metres, the circumference of one tyre. Use: Circumference of a circle = π × diameter, with π = 3,142.
subQuestions.memoText:
Diameter = 1 160 mm ÷ 1 000 = 1,16 m
Circumference = 3,142 × 1,16 = 3,64 m (accept 3,645 m)

Mark 1: converting 1 160 mm to 1,16 m
Mark 2: substituting into the formula
Mark 3: answer 3,64 m

subQuestions.questionText: The wheels of the irrigation tower move at an average rate of 2 minutes per metre. Calculate the time required to complete one full cycle around the field, given that the field has a circumference of 2,2 km. Provide your answer in hours and minutes.
subQuestions.memoText:
2,2 km = 2 200 m
Time = 2 200 m × 2 minutes per metre = 4 400 minutes
4 400 ÷ 60 = 73,33 hours
= 73 hours 20 minutes

Mark 1: converting 2,2 km to 2 200 m
Mark 2: × 2 minutes per metre
Mark 3: 4 400 minutes
Mark 4: ÷ 60
Mark 5: 73 hours 20 minutes

subQuestions.questionText: The galvanised piping used in the pivot system has an outside diameter of 17 cm, an inside diameter of 16 cm and a length of 3 500 cm. Calculate, in cm³, the inside volume of one of these galvanised pipes. Use: Volume of a cylinder = π × radius² × height, with π = 3,142.
subQuestions.memoText:
Inside radius = 16 cm ÷ 2 = 8 cm
Volume = 3,142 × 8² × 3 500
= 3,142 × 64 × 3 500
= 703 808 cm³

Mark 1: inside radius = 8 cm
Mark 2: substituting into the formula
Mark 3: answer 703 808 cm³

subQuestions.label: 3.3.2 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: Each pipe is 3 500 cm long. Calculate how many of these pipes you would need to fit together in order to make an irrigation arm of 420 metres.
subQuestions.memoText:
Pipe length = 3 500 cm = 35 m
Number of pipes = 420 m ÷ 35 m = 12 pipes

Mark 1: converting 3 500 cm to 35 m
Mark 2: dividing 420 by 35
Mark 3: answer 12 pipes

subQuestions.label: 3.3.2 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Using your answers from Question 3.3.1 (703 808 cm³ per pipe) and Question 3.3.2 (a) (12 pipes), calculate the total volume of water in these pipes if all the pipes are full to capacity. Round off your answer to the nearest kilolitre. (1 mℓ = 1 cm³; 1 kℓ = 1 000 000 cm³.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Total volume = 703 808 cm³ × 12 = 8 445 696 cm³
= 8 445 696 mℓ
= 8 445 696 ÷ 1 000 000 kℓ
= 8,445696 kℓ
≈ 8 kℓ

Mark 1: 703 808 × 12
Mark 2: 8 445 696 cm³
Mark 3: cm³ = mℓ
Mark 4: ÷ 1 000 000
Mark 5: rounding → 8 kℓ

questions.title: Nceba the Drafter — Floor Plans, Elevations, Scale and Probability

subQuestions.questionText: Nceba has created a construction drawing for a single house, showing each room from above with its name, area and floor covering (e.g. Bedr 2, 16 m², Carpet). Give the specific name of the construction drawing shown.
subQuestions.memoText:
A floor plan (also accept: house plan / blueprint).

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: Label the side marked 4.1.2 on the drawing with the correct compass direction, given that the patio is south-facing and north is at the top of the page.
subQuestions.memoText:
West

(North is at the top of the page; the patio faces south; the side marked 4.1.2 faces west.)

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: The drawing shows an overall length of 11 210 mm. Using this measurement and a ruler, calculate, to the nearest 10, the unit ratio scale of the drawing. Show all your working. (The 11 210 mm length measures about 117 mm on the printed drawing.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Measured length : real length = 117 mm : 11 210 mm
Divide both by 117:
= 1 : 95,81
≈ 1 : 100

Mark 1: measuring the length (≈ 117 mm)
Mark 2: writing the ratio 117 : 11 210 in the correct order
Mark 3: dividing both parts by 117
Mark 4: 1 : 95,81 ≈ 1 : 100

subQuestions.questionText: Give a possible reason why the bedroom doors in the main bedroom and bedroom 3 do not open into the passage.
subQuestions.memoText:
So the open doors do not block the passage (a walkway), and/or to make the best use of the space inside the bedroom. (Also acceptable: SA building regulations require bedroom doors to open inward, which is safer / easier to force open in an emergency.)

[Award 2 marks for a valid reason]

subQuestions.questionText: This drawing shows a small three-bedroom house. Identify ONE feature, other than size, of this house which could be a challenge for a family of four.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any one appropriate feature read from the plan, e.g.: only one bathroom; no garage shown; the house is not north-facing; only three bedrooms so two family members must share a room.

[Award 2 marks for one valid feature]

subQuestions.questionText: Nceba drew the side elevation for this house. The patio (south-facing) with its stacking door appears in this elevation. Circle the side of the house that is illustrated in this elevation plan.
subQuestions.memoText:
B — South elevation

[Award 2 marks for identifying the correct elevation]

subQuestions.questionText: A stacking door is shown in this (south) elevation plan. Nceba has drawn another stacking door in this house, on the side of the lounge. On which elevation plan would this second stacking door be shown?
subQuestions.memoText:
The West elevation.

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: The elevation is drawn to a scale of 1 : 100. The height of the house, shown by the line AB, measures 5 cm on the drawing. Use the scale to calculate, in metres, the actual height of the house.
subQuestions.memoText:
Actual height = 5 cm × 100 = 500 cm
500 cm ÷ 100 = 5 m

Mark 1: measuring AB (5 cm)
Mark 2: × 100 (the scale)
Mark 3: 500 cm
Mark 4: converting to 5 m

subQuestions.questionText: New homeowners can select their wall colour (Navy Blue or Grey) and roof colour (Red or Green). List all the possible combinations of wall colour and roof colour a home owner can choose from.
subQuestions.memoText:
Navy Blue and Red
Navy Blue and Green
Grey and Red
Grey and Green

[Award 1 mark per correct combination; full marks for all four with no extras]

subQuestions.questionText: The weather forecast is: Friday 10 May 2024 — max 10 °C, chance of rain 0,48; Saturday 11 May 2024 — max 17 °C, chance of rain 0,23; Sunday 12 May 2024 — max 22 °C, chance of rain 0,03. State which day has the highest chance of rainfall.
subQuestions.memoText:
Friday 10 May 2024 (chance of rain 0,48, the highest of the three).

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the percentage chance that it will NOT rain on Saturday, 11 May 2024 (chance of rain = 0,23).
subQuestions.memoText:
P(no rain) = 100% − 23% = 77%

Mark 1: subtracting 23% from 100%
Mark 2: answer 77%

subQuestions.questionText: If a day is selected randomly from the three forecast days, what is the likelihood that the maximum temperature will exceed 17 °C? (Max temperatures: 10 °C, 17 °C, 22 °C.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Only Sunday (22 °C) exceeds 17 °C.
P(temperature exceeds 17 °C) = 1/3 (≈ 0,33 / 33%) — unlikely.

Mark 1: 1 day out of 3
Mark 2: answer 1/3

questions.title: Red Frogs Road Trip — Highways, Strip Maps, Travel Time and Directions

subQuestions.questionText: Dave and his team travel by car from Johannesburg to Ballito on the KwaZulu-Natal North Coast. Using the strip map, along which two highways will Dave's team travel?
subQuestions.memoText:
The N3 and the N2

[Award 2 marks — 1 per correct highway]

subQuestions.questionText: The team will make a single stop along the N3 route to refuel and rest. Use the strip map to identify a suitable stop that will divide their journey into approximately two equal segments. Use calculations and distances to justify your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Harrismith — it is about 289 km from Durban and about 268 km from Johannesburg, so it lies roughly halfway along the route and divides the journey into two approximately equal segments.

Mark 1: identifying Harrismith
Mark 2: using the two distances to justify the choice

subQuestions.questionText: Dave and his team need to be in Ballito at 6 pm for a team meeting. The distance from Johannesburg to Durban along the N3 is 557 km and from Durban to Ballito along the N2 is 43 km. They will make one stop of 45 minutes and travel at an average speed of 100 km/h. Determine the latest time they can leave Johannesburg to get to their meeting on time. Use: Time = Distance ÷ Speed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Total distance = 557 km + 43 km = 600 km
Travelling time = 600 ÷ 100 = 6 hours
Add the 45-minute stop: 6 h + 45 min = 6 h 45 min
Latest departure = 18:00 − 6:45 = 11:15

Mark 1: 557 + 43 = 600 km
Mark 2: substituting into Time = Distance ÷ Speed
Mark 3: 600 ÷ 100
Mark 4: 6 hours
Mark 5: adding the 45-minute stop
Mark 6: 6 h 45 min
Mark 7: 18:00 − 6:45 = 11:15

subQuestions.questionText: Hop's Restaurant & Bar Ballito is on the corner of two roads. Using the map, name these two roads.
subQuestions.memoText:
Hawkins Road and Edward Place

[Award 2 marks — 1 per correct road]

subQuestions.label: 5.2.2 (a)
subQuestions.questionText: A Red Frog crew member needs to help a student get from Hop's Restaurant & Bar Ballito to their accommodation at Sibakwa Guest House. In which general direction will they need to walk?
subQuestions.memoText:
North-west (NW) — accept NNW.

[Award 2 marks]

subQuestions.label: 5.2.2 (b)
subQuestions.questionText: Using a pen or highlighter, trace on the given map the most direct route that the Red Frog crew member and the student might take to return to the Sibakwa Guest House. Describe the route you would trace.
subQuestions.memoText:
The most direct route: along Hawkins Road heading north-west, then right into Minerva Road, then left into Ballito Drive, crossing Patricia Road to Sibakwa Guest House.

Mark 1: route is the most direct option
Mark 2: route ends at Sibakwa Guest House

subQuestions.label: 5.2.2 (c)
subQuestions.questionText: Provide written directions for the route you traced, making sure to include all street names and directions.
subQuestions.memoText:
Walk along Hawkins Road heading in a north-west direction, passing Sandra Road. Turn right into Minerva Road, then left into Ballito Drive. Cross Patricia Road; Sibakwa Guest House will be on the right.

Mark 1: Hawkins Road, north-west
Mark 2: turn right into Minerva Road
Mark 3: turn left into Ballito Drive
Mark 4: cross Patricia Road — guest house on the right
